description: Jev-compatible API server for open decision models. Ollama for decision models: pull and serve 29 model families (Laya, pplx-decider, Clef, Winnow, coba...) locally or self-hosted behind /v1/systemone. The TypeSafe SDK works unchanged: set its base URL and pick an open model. CLI, desktop app, Docker, MCP server, public bench.

summary.one_liner: Ollaya is a local daemon and self-hosted API that pulls and serves open decision models (typed questions answered with calibrated probabilities in one forward pass, no text generation), exposing a Jev-compatible /v1/systemone endpoint.
keywords: run models on my own hardware
summary.what_it_does: Ollaya pulls named open decision models and serves them from a local daemon through an HTTP API that follows the TypeSafe /v1/systemone wire format, so the TypeSafe SDK and Jev clients can be pointed at it by changing the base URL. Each request supplies a state (text or JSON) and typed questions of types choice, score, and noul, and the model returns calibrated probabilities in a single forward pass rather than generated text. The CLI can run a model on a message with presets such as triage, or with custom questions via flags like --ask and --choice. The repository includes the CLI and daemon, the HTTP API crates, a model registry with resumable pulls, inference engines based on ONNX Runtime and llama.cpp for GGUF models, and a Python conversion pipeline with parity checks against PyTorch references. The README also describes a desktop app, Docker images, an MCP server, and a public benchmark, with install commands for Linux, macOS, and Windows.
use_cases: route customer messages to the right team without calling an LLM
triage support tickets and detect urgency or churn risk
approve or block agent tool calls with a fast decision model
add guardrail checks to an AI agent pipeline
self-host decision models behind a Jev or TypeSafe-compatible API
run calibrated classification locally on GPU or CPU
notable: Jev-compatible /v1/systemone API, so existing TypeSafe SDK code works after changing the base URL
Decision models return calibrated probabilities in one forward pass and never generate text
Ships 29 model families pulled by name, each with its own license noted in the README
Three-tier parity testing (K1, K2, K3) against PyTorch reference outputs
Multiple interfaces: CLI, desktop app, Docker image, MCP server, and public bench
caveats: Several bundled models have restrictive terms: nimble:9b-v3 adapter is CC BY-NC 4.0 (no commercial use), and d1 is under the LFM Open License, which excludes organizations with US$10M+ annual revenue
Linux install requires glibc 2.38 or newer (e.g. Ubuntu 24.04+)
GPU acceleration needs an NVIDIA driver of R525+ (Linux) or R527+ (Windows), and CUDA builds are listed only for x86-64 Linux and Windows
